articles.title: Before 9/11, US knew Bin Laden was a threat. India-Pakistan tensions were the bigger worry
articles.summary: US News: 9/11 has been one of the most horrifying incidents of terrorism to happen on American soil. It claimed 2,977 victims not even accounting for the colle.
articles.body: 9/11 has been one of the most horrifying incidents of terrorism to happen on American soil. It claimed 2,977 victims not even accounting for the collective trauma it resulted in.By the time four hijacked planes tore through the American skies, Washington had already spent years watching the rise of Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.The problem, as the 9/11 Commission Report makes clear that, in South Asia, American attention was repeatedly pulled towards another crisis.India and PakistanThe Commission report makes it a point to highlight that: "In the State Department, concerns about India-Pakistan tensions often crowded out attention to Afghanistan or Bin Ladin. Aware of instability and growing Islamic extremism in Pakistan, State Department officials worried most about an arms race and possible war between Pakistan and India."Washington knew Pakistan was unstable and it also knew that Islamist extremism was growing there. They also had information that Pakistan supported the Taliban and were aware of Bin Laden operating from within Afghanistan.But the possibility of an arms race, and eventually war, between two nuclear-armed neighbours kept competing for the top spot on the American agenda.After India and Pakistan conducted nuclear tests in May 1998, that competition became even harder to ignore. The Commission says the dangers of an arms race and possible war became “daily first-order concerns” for State Department officials.Bin Laden was meanwhile building something else.In February 1998, he publicly declared that killing Americans was an individual duty for Muslims who could do so. Three months later, in an interview with ABC, he warned that if what he described as American “injustice” continued, the battle would eventually move to American soil. The Commission notes that plans to attack the United States had been developing with “unwavering single-mindedness” throughout the 1990s.The problem next doorFor the United States, getting to Bin Laden meant dealing with Pakistan. The report also acknowledges that Bin Laden was well-known and a senior figure among Islamist extremists, especially those in Egypt, the Arabian Peninsula, and the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region. Yet he was just one of the barons of terrorism, not its face, till now.Bin Laden was based in Afghanistan, but the 9/11 Commission describes Pakistan as the country that held the key to his ability to use Afghanistan as a base for his campaign against the United States. Pakistan's military establishment was deeply preoccupied with its rivalry with India, particularly over Kashmir.That rivalry shaped Islamabad's calculations in Afghanistan.The Commission says Pakistani rulers saw the Taliban as potentially useful: they could impose order in Afghanistan and give Pakistan what its military planners called “strategic depth” against India. Pakistani intelligence officers probably knew in advance that Bin Laden was coming back to Afghanistan and may have facilitated his journey. The report also says Pakistani intelligence reportedly introduced him to Taliban leaders, partly in the hope that his camps could be made available for training Kashmiri militants.Bin Laden did not need Pakistan to be interested in his global jihad. He needed Pakistan's geopolitical calculations to create an environment in which he could operate.The United States understood this tension, but struggled to act on it.When terrorism became a secondary problemIn the summer before the 1998 US embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania, the State Department was heavily focused on rising tensions between India and Pakistan. The Commission says this meant Washington did not aggressively challenge Pakistan over Afghanistan and Bin Laden.At the same time, American counterterrorism officials were pushing in the opposite direction.The State Department's acting counterterrorism coordinator advised Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to designate Pakistan as a state sponsor of terrorism. His argument was that, despite assurances from Pakistan's leadership, its military intelligence service continued activities supporting international terrorism, including attacks on civilian targets in Kashmir.But the South Asia bureau opposed the recommendation.Its concern was that such a move would further damage an already sensitive relationship with Pakistan, particularly after the May 1998 nuclear tests by both India and Pakistan. Albright rejected the recommendation on August 5, 1998.Two days later, al-Qaeda bombed the US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania.In 1997, an NSC policy review had already concluded that Washington needed to pay greater attention not only to India but also to Pakistan and Afghanistan. One diplomat told the Commission that the United States effectively had “no policy” towards Afghanistan at the time.But soon after that came the nuclear tests and then the Kargil war.In May 1999, Pakistani troops infiltrated the Kargil sector of Kashmir, triggering a limited war with India. The Commission records Bruce Riedel, the NSC official responsible for Pakistan, describing Islamabad as behaving like a rogue state in two areas: backing Taliban/Bin Laden terrorism and provoking war with India.The irony was that the two problems were not actually separate.Pakistan's rivalry with India helped shape its policy towards militant groups. Those militant networks operated in an ecosystem that also sheltered the Taliban. And the Taliban provided Bin Laden with the Afghan sanctuary from which al-Qaeda could develop its war against the United States.Washington knew about Bin LadenWashington was not oblivious to the threat Bin Laden posed. The CIA was actively developing plans to capture him. The Justice Department was moving towards indicting him. In April 1998, US Ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson travelled to Afghanistan and asked the Taliban to expel him after Bin Laden's public call for Americans to be killed.The Taliban said they did not know where he was and insisted that he was not a threat to the United States.Counterterrorism officials wanted Pakistan to exert pressure on the Taliban. President Bill Clinton discussed Bin Laden with Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. Later, Clinton raised the issue directly with Gen Pervez Musharraf during his March 2000 visit to Pakistan and urged him to help capture Bin Laden.By then, however, the diplomatic problem had become deeply entrenched.Pakistan was simultaneously a potential partner against terrorism, a nuclear-armed rival of India, a supporter of the Taliban and a country whose military and intelligence establishment had relationships with militant groups.Washington needed Islamabad and that dependence limited how hard Washington was willing to push.Bin Laden became just one problem among several, in a region where another problem carried the possibility of nuclear war.The Commission's own summary of this period is telling: while the CIA and Justice Department pursued Bin Ladin, the State Department was concentrating more heavily on easing Indo-Pakistani nuclear tensions, ending the Afghan civil war and dealing with the Taliban's human-rights record than on driving Bin Laden out.By the time America fully understood the threat Bin Laden posed, 19 men had boarded four aircraft.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1950s, Florida landscapers introduced an Asian ornamental tree; decades later, soapberry bugs feeding on it had beaks about 30% shorter than those on native balloon vine
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Florida's soapberry bugs evolved shorter beaks in response to the introduction of the golden rain tree, illustrating rapid evolutionary changes and their implications.
articles.body: It was in the 1950s that Florida landscape gardeners planted the golden rain tree (Koelreuteria elegans), a non-native ornamental from Taiwan with yellow flowers and light, papery seed pods, as the UF/IFAS Assessment of Non-Native Plants and other sources on the species confirm. In what can be termed an immediate attraction to the non-native plant, the soapberry bug, which is an insect that uses its long, sharp beak to penetrate plants in search of food, started using the newly introduced tree for food. As stated in Living on Earth, the length of the beak for the bugs eating from the golden rain tree had become significantly reduced, becoming nearly 30 percent shorter than the beak of bugs eating the native balloon vine within the course of only 50 years.A 1992 study first documented the beak-length divergence between host populationsThe basis for the experiment was established in the paper 'Host Race Radiation in the Soapberry Bug: Natural History with the History,' which appeared in Evolution in 1992, written by Scott P. Carroll and Christin Boyd. In the study, the authors took a closer look at these Florida populations, using both museum material and current sampling. They found that beak length was associated with the change of the host plant over time, with insects feeding on the native balloon vine having longer beaks, and those feeding on the introduced golden rain tree having shorter, seed-piercing beaks. To ensure the fact that it was not a pre-existing condition but a recently acquired one, Carroll and Boyd made comparisons between the current populations and the museum specimens collected before the introduction of the new host plant.Beak reduction accompanied broader shifts in the bugs' development and survivalThe insects adapting to the golden rain tree showed more changes than just the reduced length of their mouthparts. Another observation made in the 1992 study is that variations were observed in development time and survival rate based on the host plant from which a particular population of bugs fed, indicating that variation in beak size was just one of several adaptations Carroll and Boyd documented. The later study conducted by Carroll et al. took these discoveries further and showed some genetically-based differences in performance when comparing insects from their native host with those from another host. With the golden rain tree producing abundant amounts of seeds on all trees grown across suburban and urban Florida, the adaptation of the bugs to this abundant and accessible host provided a good example for studying the evolution process.A 2016 follow-up study found the native-adapted ecotype had largely disappearedHowever, in 2016, a second study titled 'Adaptation to an invasive host is driving the loss of a native ecotype' was published by Meredith Cenzer in the journal Evolution, which sought to test how well the local adaptation pattern persisted in these same Florida populations. Cenzer combined field surveys with morphology and host-use data and found that bugs were still present on the native balloon vine, but their phenotypes had converged with those of the invasive-host population: the distinct, long-beaked native-adapted ecotype was essentially gone, replaced by populations that were now better adapted to the golden rain tree across the board, likely through gene flow from the invasive-host populations.The mechanism behind this may be gene flow. Bugs adapted to the golden rain tree may have hybridized with balloon vine populations enough to reduce the prevalence of genes associated with the long-beaked form, regardless of whether balloon vine disappeared from the environment. However, more recent research on this system indicates that maladaptive plasticity also contributed to the development of this scenario, suggesting that gene flow alone is not the only explanation. Together, the two studies show how quickly evolutionary patterns can shift and then reverseTogether, the two studies serve as an example of how quickly natural selection can drive a significant physical change, and of how quickly that change can be undone by gene flow rather than by a genuine reversal. While the earlier study traced the evolution of differences in beak length within just a few decades of the golden rain tree's introduction, the later study found that the short-beaked, invasive-adapted form had instead spread through the whole regional population, swamping and erasing the longer-beaked native-adapted ecotype rather than the population reverting to it. As far as evolutionary biology is concerned, the soapberry bug example can serve as a good one for consideration since it demonstrates both aspects of evolution in a rather easy-to-follow system.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, UNICEF began turning discarded shipping containers into solar-powered digital classrooms in Cameroon; the pilot later reached nearly 20,000 students and 284 teachers
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a groundbreaking initiative, UNICEF Cameroon has transformed discarded shipping containers into solar-powered digital classrooms, providing access to modern learning tools for over 20,000 students and teachers in underserved regions. This innovative project, launched as part of the Connect My School initiative, aims to enhance educational opportunities and bridge the digital divide in Cameroon.
articles.body: Starting in 2021, UNICEF Cameroon began converting discarded shipping containers into solar-powered digital classrooms as part of an initiative called Connect My School, aiming to bring internet access and modern learning tools to schools that had never had either. Made mostly out of used materials, the modified containers, which are referred to in the area as "e-containers," opened doors for almost 20,000 children and 284 teachers in underprivileged areas in the country during the pilot phase of the project, according to a press release by UNICEF Cameroon.The Connect My School initiative launched in April 2021 at a school in MelenThe program was launched in April 2021 at a public school in Melen, Yaoundé, led by Cameroon's Ministry of Basic Education together with UNICEF, according to an official account published by UNICEF Cameroon. The initiative's pilot phase was set to extend digital hubs to 17 schools across urban, peri-urban and rural areas, using an "e-container" built from recycled shipping materials and powered by solar energy, a design chosen for both cost and practicality in regions without a reliable electricity grid. UNICEF said the broader goal was to reach nearly 70,000 primary pupils and 4,000 out-of-school adolescents and children with disabilities in five municipalities ahead of the 2021/22 school year. In several locations, the solar setup also supplied electricity to surrounding school buildings, giving entire school compounds power they had not previously had.The pilot phase reached schools across three regions of CameroonOver the years following launch, the pilot phase expanded the e-container model into 17 schools in Cameroon's Eastern region, along with one school group each in the Central and Littoral regions, according to a UNICEF Cameroon press release marking the inauguration of an e-container at Mokolo Primary School in Bertoua in March 2024. In total, the pilot phase gave around 20,000 primary students and 284 teachers their first classroom exposure to information and communications technology. These boxes usually contain laptops or tablets, software that enables offline learning, and an internet connection if possible, in order to ensure that lessons can continue irrespective of poor broadband connection. Training of teachers who were involved in this project was conducted to familiarize them with the use of this technology, a process which UNICEF has continued in further phases of the project.The hubs gave students and teachers their first structured access to digital toolsFor many of the children involved, the e-containers marked their first hands-on experience with computers or tablets in an educational setting. At the Mokolo site in Bertoua, the local e-container served 1,116 pupils between the ages of 6 and 12, with 34 teachers trained in basic ICT instruction. As mentioned in the above release, the broader Eastern region rollout alone accounted for the bulk of the nearly 20,000 pupils reached during the pilot phase. The initiative's design also reflected a practical response to Cameroon's uneven school infrastructure. Traditional classrooms in many of the targeted communities faced overcrowding, aging equipment, and limited access to reliable power, conditions that made a self-contained, solar-powered unit a more realistic near-term solution than a full renovation of existing school buildings, though the units brought their own capacity limits once demand outpaced the number of containers available, as later sections describe.By 2024 and 2025, the pilot phase had reached its planned regions, short of its original 2021 targetBy 2024 and 2025, the model that started at Melen had grown into the wider regional rollout described above, with UNICEF continuing to document its reach through releases such as the Mokolo Primary School inauguration. In Melong, reports in 2024 showed that the local digital center was used by more than 2,900 children from ten different schools in the area, according to a UNICEF Cameroon story on the e‑container’s impact. This growth has also brought about several problems. As the number of containers increased, the number of pupils to the number of centers in some places was relatively large, to the extent that even teachers had to divide their classes into smaller groups in order to use the facilities.The solution provides the benefits of electricity and connectivity without having to invest in the construction of entire classrooms from scratch. It remains unclear whether the solution can be expanded to all schools in Cameroon, given financial constraints and the challenge of connecting more remote schools to solar power and internet access. At the same time, the pilot's first years show that a solar-powered, self-contained classroom can extend digital access to schools that previously had none, even as questions remain about funding the model's expansion.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Ryan: The 13-year-old who turns thousands of empty cans collected from homes and businesses into money for charities across the West Midlands
articles.summary: UK News: A 13-year-old boy has turned thousands of discarded drink cans into a regular source of funding for food banks and charities in the West Midlands. Rya.
articles.body: A 13-year-old boy has turned thousands of discarded drink cans into a regular source of funding for food banks and charities in the West Midlands. Ryan came up with the idea after wanting to use his spare time to help people in need. What began as a simple collection project has grown into a community effort, with residents and businesses saving bags of aluminium cans for his family to collect. Around 20,000 cans are gathered each week and taken to the family's Solihull garage, where they are crushed and sold as scrap. The money raised after costs is then donated to good causes.How a 13-year-old turned cans into a charity projectAccording to BBC reports, Ryan's project operates through We Can CIC, a Community Interest Company set up around the collection and recycling of aluminium drink cans. The 13-year-old wanted something he could do in his spare time to support people and eventually settled on collecting cans as a practical way to raise funds.The scale of the work is now considerably larger than a typical weekend project. People and businesses gather their empty cans into bags, which Ryan's family then collects. The material is taken to the family's garage in Solihull, where the cans are crushed and prepared for sale.His father, John, helps with the processing and said the operation can take as much as 20 hours a week. The family handles roughly a tonne of cans each month, turning what would otherwise enter the waste stream into a source of income for charitable causes.20,000 cans collected every week from homes and businessesThe initiative aims to collect about 20,000 cans every seven days. That figure depends on contributions from members of the public as well as businesses that save their empty containers for the family.Once the cans arrive, they have to be sorted and crushed before being taken to scrapyards. The family does not simply pass the full value of the metal on to charities, as there are costs involved in running the operation. What remains is donated to good causes.John said the family has received substantial support from people in the community and is willing to continue expanding the collection. For residents with bags of aluminium drink cans, the arrangement offers a way to have them removed while directing their value towards local support services.The scheme has also taken on an added relevance in Birmingham, where disruption to household recycling collections has left residents dealing with accumulated recyclable waste during the bin workers' strike.Money from cans helps Anawim support women in BirminghamAs reported, the recycling operation raises about £5,000 in cash and food for charities each year. Among the organisations receiving support is Anawim, a Birmingham-based women's support hub.For Anawim, the benefit goes beyond the money generated from the cans. The collection work gives some of its supporters something practical to do during the week, while the resulting funds and food help maintain its food bank supplies.Megan Heath from Anawim said the donations help keep the food bank stocked. She also described the can collecting as a useful activity for people involved with the organisation, giving them a regular task and a sense of purpose during their days.Volunteers help keep the collection movingThe system relies on more than Ryan and his family. People connected with the charities also collect cans themselves before handing them over for processing.One volunteer, Angela, who is known to friends as Miss P, spends weekdays picking up discarded cans with a litter picker and bin bags. She collects from Monday to Friday, helping turn litter from streets and other areas into material that can eventually be sold.For her, the work has become worthwhile both because of the practical result and because other women benefit from what the collection produces.An empty can is picked up, stored with others, transported to the garage, crushed and sold as scrap. The money left after expenses then makes its way towards food and other support for people using local charities.A simple recycling idea becomes regular support for local charitiesJohn said recycling is something the community wants to do more of, while the family's experience has shown there is also a financial use for material that might otherwise be treated simply as rubbish.That combination has allowed Ryan's original idea to develop into a regular operation involving residents, businesses, volunteers, his family and local charities. The garage remains an important part of it, despite the amount of work involved in processing thousands of cans.For Ryan, the starting point was much smaller. He wanted to use some of his free time to help people in need and began looking for an idea that could make a difference. The answer turned out to be something many people would normally empty, crush and throw away.Now thousands of those cans pass through the family each week, with their scrap value helping support food banks and other services in the Birmingham and Solihull area.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1999, Steven Spielberg and Kate Capshaw bought a 2.8-acre Los Angeles horse ranch for $5.75 million; 27 years later, their seven-bedroom equestrian estate with a 20,000-sq-ft riding arena is seeking $29.9 million
articles.summary: News News: In 1999, filmmaker Steven Spielberg and his wife, Kate Capshaw, purchased a sprawling ranch in Los Angeles through their corporate entity, Texas Tart,.
articles.body: In 1999, filmmaker Steven Spielberg and his wife, Kate Capshaw, purchased a sprawling ranch in Los Angeles through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million. Now, according to a report by Realtor.com, the couple has listed the property for nearly $30 million, decades after abandoning controversial plans to transform it with an enormous five-story riding facility.At the time, the Hollywood mogul, 79 and actress, 72, unveiled ambitious plans to dramatically overhaul the estate with a 27,000-square-foot, five-story riding facility featuring a domed roof and underground horse stables. The 'Jaws' director also reportedly envisioned more than $7 million worth of renovations, along with plans to construct a 2,400-square-foot guesthouse and a three-story guardhouse.However, the proposed transformation sparked a fierce backlash from their neighbours, who objected to the scale of the project. Although the Oscar-winning director reportedly planned to present revised ideas to his neighbours, the elaborate project ultimately never came to fruition. However, he did get a chance to update the estate into the magnificent abode it is today.The property has remained a part of Spielberg and Capshaw's extensive real estate portfolio for nearly three decades. Now, the couple is finally ready to part ways with the equestrian retreat, listing it for $29.9 million with Sandro Dazzan of The Agency.Known as Dogwood, the seven-bedroom, 9.5-bathroom estate sits on 2.8 acres in the ultra-private Sullivan Canyon and offers an impressive array of equestrian amenities alongside its luxurious living spaces. Spanning two parcels, the property combines a sophisticated country-inspired aesthetic with extensive facilities designed for horses, entertaining and guests. Inside the main residence, rich walnut floors and wood-covered ceilings create a warm atmosphere, while expansive windows bring in plenty of natural light.The spacious living room offers multiple seating areas anchored by dual fireplaces, creating an inviting space for relaxing and entertaining. The chef's kitchen features extensive wood cabinetry, an oversized centre island, high-end appliances and an eat-in dining nook. "The chef's kitchen with eat-in dining nook and wood-burning fireplace connects to a cosy family room and IPE-clad terrace overlooking a tranquil reflection pond," the listing notes.Upstairs, the primary suite offers a peaceful retreat complete with a wood-burning fireplace and access to a private covered terrace. The outdoor space boasts yet another fireplace along with sweeping city and canyon views, according to the listing. Elsewhere inside the home is a media room that can double as a game room, as well as a wine cellar.Apart from all this, the property's most impressive feature is its four-legged residents. Across from the main entertaining spaces sits a six-stall barn complete with an executive office, staff quarters, three grooming stations, a feed kitchen and storage. The equestrian facility is topped off by a sprawling 20,000-square-foot riding arena with an observation deck and mirrored wall, which the listing notes is suitable for both dressage and jumping.The estate's lower parcel expands the compound even further with a stylish one-bedroom guesthouse equipped with its own kitchen, rooftop deck, and basement office and storage spaces. There is also a second four-stall barn, a 5,400-square-foot turnout area, a private gate, and enough parking for more than 10 vehicles. Both parcels are supported by a security command post and generators, further adding to the property's private compound-like feel.Outside, the ranch is surrounded by lush landscaping, while a tranquil reflection pond adds to its secluded, countryside atmosphere, despite the estate's location in the heart of Los Angeles."Nestled in the ultra-private Sullivan Canyon, Dogwood is Los Angeles' premier equestrian ranch - a rare masterpiece designed by renowned architect Michael Kovac with interiors by Michael Smith and landscape design by Christine London," the listing states.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Delhi man goes for infertility test, doctors find uterus, testes inside abdomen
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 26-year-old man who approached RG Hospitals in Rajouri Garden for infertility treatment was found to have a uterus and fallopian-tube-lik.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 26-year-old man who approached RG Hospitals in Rajouri Garden for infertility treatment was found to have a uterus and fallopian-tube-like structures inside his body, revealing a rare congenital condition that had remained undiagnosed until adulthood, news agency ANI reported.The man was seeking treatment for primary infertility and was found to have azoospermia, or absence of sperm in semen. Doctors also found that both his testes were undescended. Further evaluation, including imaging and genetic testing, was carried out to determine the underlying cause.An MRI scan showed a uterus-like structure in the pelvis along with structures resembling fallopian tubes. Genetic testing showed a 46,XY chromosome pattern, leading doctors to suspect Persistent Mullerian Duct Syndrome (PMDS), a rare congenital condition in which Mullerian structures such as the uterus and fallopian tubes persist in a person with typically male chromosomes and physical development.Laparoscopic exploration confirmed a small, underdeveloped uterus and tubular Mullerian structures associated with both testes, which were located inside the abdomen. The testes were severely damaged and atrophied.Doctors subsequently removed the Mullerian structures and both testes through laparoscopic surgery, considering the patient's age, long-standing undescended testes, severe testicular damage and increased risk of testicular cancer.The surgery was performed by Dr Susheel Kharbanda, chief urologist at RG Hospitals, Rajouri Garden."This was an extremely unusual case because the patient came to us with infertility, and the underlying condition had remained undiagnosed until adulthood. The evaluation showed that he had a persistent Mullerian structure along with both testes located inside the abdomen," Dr Kharbanda said."The testes were also severely atrophied, which was an important concern because undescended testes carry a higher risk of testicular cancer. We therefore had to approach the surgery carefully, taking into account both the unusual anatomy and the long-term health risks," he said.The most significant finding emerged during microscopic examination of the removed tissue. Both testes were severely atrophied, while the left testis showed Germ Cell Neoplasia In Situ (GCNIS), a pre-cancerous change that can develop into testicular cancer.The right testis showed severe atrophy but no evidence of GCNIS. Blood tests for common testicular tumour markers were normal.The case highlights that normal tumour-marker levels do not necessarily rule out early or pre-cancerous changes, particularly in patients with long-standing undescended testes.PMDS is usually detected earlier in life, often when a child is evaluated or treated for an undescended testis. Its first detection in adulthood during an infertility evaluation is uncommon. In this case, an investigation into male infertility led doctors to uncover both the rare congenital condition and an unexpected cancer risk.The case also highlights the need to investigate unexplained infertility when it occurs alongside bilateral undescended testes. Imaging, genetic testing, laparoscopic examination and detailed tissue analysis helped doctors identify the condition and the pre-cancerous change.RG Hospitals said the case was managed through a multidisciplinary approach involving urology, radiology, pathology, reproductive medicine and endocrinology. The team used imaging, genetic evaluation, minimally invasive surgery and histopathology to diagnose the condition and address the associated oncological risk.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Pickaxe Mountain next? New activity at US bunker-buster test site fuels speculation
articles.summary: International News: Construction work at an obscure underground weapons test site in New Mexico is drawing fresh attention, with CNN reporting the activity may be tied to.
articles.body: Construction work at an obscure underground weapons test site in New Mexico is drawing fresh attention, with CNN reporting the activity may be tied to planning for a potential future strike on Iran's toughest nuclear facility, Pickaxe Mountain, a site the US and Israel have notably left untouched through multiple rounds of strikes so far.The link traces back to February 27, the day before the initial wave of US-Israeli strikes on Iran, when the Pentagon's Defense Threat Reduction Agency (DTRA) quietly awarded a sole-source contract to Pate Construction for work at the Alternate Seismic Hardrock in Situ Test (ALT-SHIST) site, tucked inside the sprawling White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico's Jornada del Muerto desert. DTRA, a relatively low-profile agency, leads US military efforts on countering weapons of mass destruction. The agency helped develop the 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, the bunker-buster bomb that made its combat debut striking Iran's underground facilities at Fordow and Natanz during Operation Midnight Hammer, after being extensively tested at White Sands beforehand.There's speculation a different site within the same range may have been used to rehearse the actual Fordow strike plan, which involved slamming six GBU-57s in rapid succession into each of two ventilation shafts, burrowing progressively deeper with every hit. Notably, White Sands also holds the site of the world's first atomic bomb test in 1945.DTRA's official justification for the February contract made no mention of Iran, citing only an urgent national security requirement, and caution is warranted since ALT-SHIST is a continuously active site with other ongoing projects, including separate work on its Tunnel 7 section dating back to last year. The facility, established in 1995 as a successor to the original 1993 SHIST site, is just one of several hardened-target test ranges DTRA operates within White Sands. Whether or not this particular contract relates to Pickaxe Mountain specifically remains unconfirmed, but the site's continued survival through several rounds of US and Israeli strikes keeps it firmly in the conversation.

articles.title: Putin, Xi and a bigger Brics: India becomes the stage for high-stakes global diplomacy test
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Delhi has been turned into a fortress. Roads are being secured, security has been stepped up and the capital is preparing for the arrival o.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi has been turned into a fortress. Roads are being secured, security has been stepped up and the capital is preparing for the arrival of some of the world’s most powerful leaders.Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and other leaders are set to gather for the Brics Summit, turning New Delhi into the stage for a meeting of a bloc that now represents nearly half of the world’s population.But beyond the motorcades, bilateral meetings and summit optics lies a much bigger test. With 49.5% of the world’s population, Brics is no longer simply a grouping of emerging economies. As India hosts the 18th Brics Summit on September 12-13, New Delhi now has to show what it can do with that growing weight.India has spent its 2026 chairship pushing the grouping towards more practical cooperation: from food and energy security to critical supply chains, artificial intelligence and development finance. The challenge now is whether those efforts can translate into meaningful outcomes at a time when wars, tariff battles, supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical rivalries are reshaping the global economy.A bigger Brics, a bigger global footprintBrics began with Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2011. The grouping expanded significantly in 2024 with the addition of Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Indonesia joined in 2025, taking the number of full members to 11.The bloc also has 10 partner countries: Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.The expansion has dramatically widened Brics’ geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. It brings together major energy producers, manufacturing powers, large consumer markets, commodity exporters and rapidly developing economies.Diversity is both an asset and a challenge. Brics has emerged as an important platform for major emerging economies to coordinate positions on global governance, development, trade, finance and technology. Its members also use the grouping to press for greater representation of developing countries in institutions such as the IMF, World Bank and UN.Yet the same diversity makes consensus more difficult. Unlike a formal economic union, Brics has neither a single economic policy nor a common foreign policy. Its members have different political systems, economic structures and strategic interests, and in some cases, sharply divergent positions on major international issues.The West Asia crisis is a particularly difficult test. Iran and the UAE are both members of Brics but have differing positions on the conflict. Saudi Arabia is also part of the grouping, adding another layer of complexity to attempts to craft a common political response.With Brics functioning on the principle of consensus, India faces the delicate task of finding language that can accommodate competing national positions while still producing a meaningful summit declaration.India’s four prioritiesResilienceThe resilience pillar focuses on strengthening the ability of BRICS economies to withstand disruptions in the global economy. The agenda includes health, agriculture, food security, energy security, disaster risk reduction and critical supply chains.The focus reflects lessons from the pandemic, geopolitical conflicts and disruptions to global trade and logistics. For emerging economies, disruptions in energy supplies, food markets, shipping routes or access to essential industrial inputs can quickly translate into inflation, shortages and slower growth.India has therefore sought greater cooperation among BRICS countries to build more resilient and diversified supply chains, alongside stronger trade, investment and connectivity.InnovationThe second pillar focuses on innovation and emerging technologies. India has highlighted digital public infrastructure, fintech, artificial intelligence and knowledge-sharing as tools that can help Brics economies improve public services and create new opportunities for growth.For New Delhi, the emphasis is not simply on technological advancement but on using technology for inclusive development.India is seeking to showcase its experience with digital public infrastructure while encouraging cooperation in areas where emerging technologies can support health, agriculture, financial inclusion, disaster management and public service delivery.The larger objective is to make Brics cooperation more relevant to citizens rather than confining it to government-to-government discussions.CooperationThe third pillar seeks to deepen practical cooperation through policy coordination, development finance, trade facilitation, investment, connectivity and reform of global institutions.External affairs minister S Jaishankar has said Brics must move from being a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery.That approach is reflected in the range of meetings held during India’s chairship, including ministerial engagements and discussions involving business, technology and other stakeholders. India has also sought to strengthen people-to-people exchanges and broaden participation beyond political leaders and government officials.SustainabilityThe fourth pillar is sustainability, with a focus on climate action, green finance, energy transition and sustainable development. For Brics economies, the challenge is particularly complex: many are simultaneously dealing with rising energy demand, development needs and pressure to reduce emissions.India has therefore placed emphasis on finding practical pathways that balance economic growth with climate objectives, while recognising the different development levels and energy requirements of member countries.Brics and India’s Global South pitchAt its core, Brics has evolved into a platform for emerging economies seeking a greater say in the institutions that shape the global economic and political order. Its members argue that the distribution of influence in institutions such as the IMF and World Bank does not adequately reflect the economic weight of developing countries today.India has consistently backed reforms to global governance institutions, including greater representation for developing countries. But New Delhi’s approach is not one of replacing the existing global economic system with a new bloc-based order.India continues to maintain deep economic, technological and strategic relationships with Western economies while participating in groupings such as the Quad and G20.For New Delhi, Brics is therefore a tool of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment a platform through which India can work with China, Russia, Gulf countries, Africa and Latin America while simultaneously expanding its engagement with the US, Europe and other partners.It also strengthens India’s credentials as a leading voice of the Global South.The economic storyThe economic weight of Brics is perhaps its most obvious strength. According to figures cited by the Indian government, the 11-member grouping accounts for around 49.5% of the world’s population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade.India’s total goods trade with Brics members more than doubled from $203.1 billion in FY21 to $417.5 billion in FY26, according to data cited by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).But the numbers also expose a major challenge for New Delhi: the rapid growth of imports has far outpaced exports. India’s exports to Brics increased 48.8%, from $64.3 billion in FY21 to $95.7 billion in FY26. Imports, meanwhile, jumped 131.8%, from $138.8 billion to $321.8 billion.As a result, India’s trade deficit with Brics more than tripled, rising from $74.5 billion to $226.1 billion. The BRICS share in India’s exports fell marginally from 22% to 21.7%, while its share in India’s imports rose sharply from 35.2% to 41.5%.UAE is India’s biggest Brics export marketWithin the expanded grouping, the UAE emerged as India’s largest export market in FY26. India exported goods worth $37.4 billion to the UAE, up 124% from FY21.China was the second-largest destination at $19.5 billion, followed by Saudi Arabia at $10.3 billion. Brazil and South Africa accounted for around $7 billion each, while exports to Russia and Indonesia stood at around $4.5 billion each.India’s exports declined to Indonesia, Iran and Ethiopia. On the import side, however, China remained India’s largest Brics supplier. Indian imports from China doubled from $65.2 billion to $131.6 billion, accounting for about 41% of India’s Brics imports.The UAE supplied goods worth $63.9 billion, while imports from Russia increased more than tenfold, from $5.5 billion to $55.4 billion, primarily because of higher energy purchases.China, the UAE and Russia together accounted for almost 84% of India’s imports from Brics. For India, the challenge is therefore not simply to increase trade with Brics but to make that trade more balanced.GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said the priority should be to correct the growing imbalance. “Brics is becoming an increasingly important source of machinery, industrial inputs, energy and commodities. However, it is not absorbing a comparable share of Indian exports,” said.“India should seek better market access in China, Russia and Indonesia, address non-tariff barriers, promote higher-value exports and reduce excessive dependence on a few Brics suppliers. Without stronger export growth, deeper intra-BRICS trade could further widen India's already large trade deficit,” he added.The broader Brics trade numbers tell another story. GTRI estimates that Brics countries exported around $1.1 trillion worth of goods to one another, equivalent to 18.8% of their combined global exports.Their imports from fellow Brics countries stood at around $1.4 trillion, representing 29.5% of their global imports. This means BRICS economies remain more important to one another as sources of imports than as export destinations.China is the dominant player. In 2025, Brics countries exported goods worth around $5.67 trillion, accounting for 21.6% of global exports. Their imports totalled approximately $4.58 trillion, or 17.3% of global imports.China alone exported $550.8 billion to other Brics members and imported $464.9 billion from them.China’s manufacturing scale, export capacity and role in global supply chains make it the economic anchor of Brics. For commodity-producing members, China provides a major market. For countries such as India and Brazil, the bloc provides opportunities for diversification and greater collective bargaining power.But it also means Brics integration cannot be understood simply as a partnership among equals.For the grouping to become a genuinely integrated economic force, the next stage would require deeper business-to-business connections, greater investment flows and stronger institutional links.The Trump factorIndia’s Brics presidency has another powerful observer: US President Donald Trump.As Brics leaders gather in New Delhi against the backdrop of the Iran war, disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, trade tensions and a rapidly shifting global economy, Washington will be watching closely. Each of these issues intersects with US interests, from energy prices and shipping routes to tariffs, the dollar and the changing balance of global power.Trump has repeatedly targeted Brics over its efforts to reduce dependence on the US dollar, portraying the grouping as a challenge to American economic dominance.“You have this little group called Brics. It's fading out fast, but BRICS is, they wanted to try and take over the dollar, the dominance of the dollar, and the standard of the dollar,” Trump told reporters at the White House last year in July.He also warned: “Any Country aligning themselves with the Anti-American policies of Brics, will be charged an ADDITIONAL 10% Tariff. There will be no exceptions to this policy. Thank you for your attention to this matter!”In October 2025, Trump described Brics’ de-dollarisation efforts as an “attack on the dollar” and again threatened tariffs against countries joining the grouping.“I told anybody who wants to be in Brics, that's fine, but we're going to put tariffs on your nation,” he said in the Oval Office.The Troika: India, Russia and ChinaThe geopolitical backdrop has made the Brics summit even more consequential. At the recent Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin projected an unusually warm display of strategic camaraderie.PM Modi described Russia as a “special and privileged partner”, while Xi said “the world’s two most populous countries need to be friends.” Putin, meanwhile, referred to Modi as his “dear friend” and travelled with him in his armoured Aurus limousine.The optics came at a particularly sensitive moment for Washington. The Trump administration has sought to prevent Russia and China from developing an even closer strategic partnership. Trump himself has said: “The one thing you never want to happen is… Russia and China uniting. I’m going to have to un-unite them, and I think I can do that.”The logic echoes the strategy of former US president Richard Nixon, whose 1972 opening to China exploited the Sino-Soviet split and transformed the Cold War balance.The emerging picture today, however, is markedly different. Rather than driving Russia away from China, Washington’s efforts have coincided with Moscow maintaining close ties with Beijing while simultaneously deepening its relationship with New Delhi.Italian analyst Francesco Sisci described the dynamic as a “Reverse Nixon”.“The Nixon paradigm did work in reverse, but differently from what the US had thought; that is, Moscow played Washington this time,” he added.The significance goes beyond symbolism. Russia has emerged as an important supplier of energy and defence equipment to India, while China remains India’s largest trading partner and a major economic power within Brics.Xi’s India visit adds another layerChinese President Xi Jinping will also visit India for the Brics summit, marking his first visit to the country in seven years. His participation is significant not only for Brics but also for the gradual improvement in India-China ties following the 2020 eastern Ladakh military standoff.PM Modi and Xi have held several meetings since their 2024 interaction on the sidelines of the Brics summit in Kazan, which marked a further easing of tensions and the resolution of issues related to disengagement.The two sides have also resumed high-level engagement on the boundary question.For India, the Brics summit provides an opportunity to push for fair market access, reliable supply chains and greater balance in bilateral trade, while maintaining its position that peace and tranquillity along the border are essential for the broader development of ties.For China, the summit is equally important because Beijing will take over the Brics chairship after India.Iran, UAE and the test of consensusIf the economic agenda tests Brics’ ability to deliver, the Middle East crisis is testing its ability to reach consensus. Iran is a full member of Brics. So are the UAE and Saudi Arabia, countries with their own strategic interests in the region.India is seeking language that emphasises the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection.The Strait of Hormuz adds particular urgency because any prolonged disruption could affect global energy markets, shipping costs and inflation.The challenge is to ensure that disagreements over the conflict do not derail the broader economic agenda. If consensus on political language proves difficult, New Delhi may seek to insulate economic agreements from contentious geopolitical issues by acknowledging individual national positions.The India challenge: Making a bigger Brics workThe rapid expansion of Brics has increased its global influence but also raised questions about governability.Prof Srikanth Kondapalli of Jawaharlal Nehru University has described the transformation as significant, pointing to the growing geographical spread and increasing number of countries seeking closer association with the grouping.He believes India is attempting to make Brics cooperation more decentralised and practical by taking the agenda beyond leaders and ministers to businesses, startups and civil society.“This is a new format that India is trying to pursue a decentralisation process compared to many centralised initiatives,” Kondapalli told ANI.He pointed to cooperation in areas including agriculture, startups, climate finance and artificial intelligence, arguing that these could help developing economies cope with international shocks.At the same time, he warned that further expansion could make consensus-building more difficult.“There is no organisation which is intercontinental other than the United Nations. Brics has over these two decades established itself as an intercontinental organisation,” he said.The challenge for India is therefore to ensure that a larger Brics does not become a less effective Brics.What India wants from the summitIndia’s priorities for the summit extend beyond the headline political issues. Among the areas expected to receive attention are trade, investment, development finance, resilient supply chains, cross-border payments, startups, technology, sustainability and global governance reform.India also wants continued support for issues such as UN Security Council reform and counter-terrorism cooperation.The proposed outcomes are aimed at giving the chairship a practical legacy. The summit is expected to culminate in the release of the New Delhi Declaration, although reaching consensus on the document remains one of the key diplomatic challenges.According to the ministry of external affairs schedule, the summit will begin on Saturday afternoon with a closed-door session for Brics member countries on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.”The leaders will subsequently visit the Bharat Innovates Exhibition, followed by a family photograph and joint tree-planting ceremony. Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders on Saturday evening.On Sunday, the leaders will attend the open session titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.” The summit will conclude with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.India’s multi-alignment in sharper focusFor India, the message is less about choosing and more about preserving strategic room to manoeuvre. Recent diplomatic activity has underscored that approach. PM Modi met Xi in China and held talks with Putin, while also maintaining engagement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.The Russia relationship remains particularly important because of energy. According to Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, India’s energy imports from Russia have reached record levels.“I don’t want to give you any figures for understandable reasons, but every month we have a new record,” he said.Peskov also said Russia remained committed to fulfilling its defence commitments to India, including deliveries of the S-400 Triumf air defence systems.“Russia is capable of fulfilling its obligations, and they will be fulfilled. This issue is being mentioned during the conversations of our two leaders,” Peskov added.Moscow is also exploring deeper cooperation with India in areas including rare earths and the potential sale of Su-57 fighter jets, according to Peskov.On Ukraine, he suggested that Moscow sees considerable convergence with New Delhi. “We know India’s position on the Ukrainian conflict, and to a great extent... it corresponds with our own position, because we do want the resolution of the Ukrainian conflict by peaceful means, and Russia is open to this process,” Peskov said.The tariff factorThe relationship with Washington, meanwhile, has become more complicated. Trump’s tariff policy has added an economic dimension to what was already a difficult geopolitical balancing act.For India, the concern is that pressure over trade could spill into wider strategic ties. At the same time, India’s growing closeness to Moscow and renewed engagement with Beijing do not necessarily signal a break with Washington.As Sreeram Sundar Chaulia of the Jindal School of International Affairs put it, India could still seek to maintain both relationships, “the Russian cake and eating the American pie”, but trust with Washington would be crucial.Russia has rejected the suggestion that Brics is pursuing formal de-dollarisation. Peskov said the grouping was not considering such a move, while criticising the use of national currencies as instruments of political pressure and calling proposed US sanctions illegal and unacceptable.India’s position is broadly consistent with this distinction: greater financial diversification is not the same as replacing the dollar.Why Brics matters to IndiaDespite its political differences and economic imbalances, Brics remains strategically important to India.The grouping gives New Delhi a platform to work with China, Russia, Gulf countries, Africa and Latin America while continuing its engagement with the US, Europe, the Quad and other Western partners.It also strengthens India’s claim to a leadership role in the Global South. Working alongside major emerging economies, India can push for reforms of institutions such as the UN Security Council, IMF and World Bank, whose structures are widely seen as insufficiently representative of the developing world.Support within Brics for reform of the UN system is significant, although it falls short of an explicit endorsement of India’s bid for permanent membership of the Security Council, an issue complicated by China’s position.The China factor remains central. Stepping away from Brics would risk leaving greater space for Beijing to shape the economic and political agenda of the developing world. India’s presence allows it to push for a more balanced approach and resist any attempt to turn Brics into an explicitly anti-Western platform.Building alternatives without targeting dollarFinancial cooperation is another important pillar. Institutions such as the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) demonstrate Brics’ ability to build mechanisms of its own.India supports greater use of local currencies for legitimate trade and settlement, but has opposed the idea of a common Brics currency or a China-dominated alternative to the existing financial system.The economic case is equally important. Brics provides India with access to large markets while creating opportunities for trade diversification, supply-chain resilience and de-risking.Its membership also deepens India’s economic ties with major energy suppliers such as Russia, agricultural and commodity producers such as Brazil, and Gulf and African economies.From dialogue to deliveryJaishankar, while announcing India’s Brics summit, said the grouping must now move “from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery.”That objective is reflected in India’s focus on concrete outcomes for the New Delhi summit, including a Brics declaration, a logistics and supply-chain cooperation framework, startup and incubator networks, development finance, cross-border payments, and continued support for priorities such as UN Security Council reform and counterterrorism.India has some reason for confidence when it comes to navigating difficult multilateral negotiations.At the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi, the inclusion of the African Union as a permanent member was a major diplomatic achievement. Equally significant was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine, where India helped broker compromise language that enabled leaders to adopt a joint declaration despite deep divisions over the war.That experience could prove valuable as New Delhi prepares for another difficult summit involving an even more diverse set of political and economic interests.A 20-year-old grouping at a turning pointBrics has travelled a long way from the acronym coined by Goldman Sachs to describe emerging economies with high growth potential.UNCTAD estimates that Brics members’ global merchandise exports rose from nearly $1 trillion in 2003 to around $6 trillion in 2024, while their share of global exports doubled from approximately 12% to 24%.Yet economic size alone does not create an integrated bloc. The growth of intra-Brics trade has been substantial, but investment and deeper business links remain less developed than the bloc’s headline economic numbers might suggest.Brics has created political visibility, expanded South-South trade and established institutions such as the NDB. It has also strengthened calls for greater representation of emerging economies in global governance.The next test is whether that weight can be converted into deeper cooperation and tangible results.From a platform to a forceFor India, the opportunity lies in using Brics to make the Global South’s economic weight count more effectively without turning the grouping into an anti-Western alliance.That requires navigating several contradictions at once. India must work with China without allowing Beijing’s economic dominance to dictate the agenda. It must deepen ties with Russia while managing its increasingly important relationship with the US.It must push for local-currency trade without turning the dollar debate into a confrontation. And it must build consensus among countries whose interests can diverge sharply, particularly on issues such as West Asia.The economic challenge is equally clear. India needs Brics markets, but it also needs to ensure that greater integration does not deepen its trade deficit. It needs access to Chinese and other Brics markets while reducing excessive dependence on a handful of suppliers.At a time of wars, tariff battles, supply-chain disruptions and a rapidly changing global order, this is perhaps the biggest test yet for a bloc that began as an economic acronym and has grown into an important geopolitical platform. Brics has grown bigger. India’s task is to make it more effective.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Suvendu Adhikari eats fish bhog at Kalighat amid Bageshwar Baba row: What sparked the controversy
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday visited Kolkata's Kalighat Temple and partook of the traditional fish and pulao bho.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday visited Kolkata's Kalighat Temple and partook of the traditional fish and pulao bhog, days after Dhirendra Krishna Shastri triggered a row by asking Bengalis to give up non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja.The visit came as the controversy over Shastri’s remarks continued to grow, with leaders across parties, including the BJP, pushing back against alleged attempts to dictate Bengal’s food habits.Speaking to reporters after offering prayers, Adhikari described Kaushiki Amavasya as a significant occasion in Sanatan culture and said that the festival was being observed with devotion at major temples across the state, including Kalighat and Tarapith."Today is Kaushiki Amavasya. Today is a very big day in our Sanatan culture, a major worship (Mahapuja). Whether it is Kalighat here or Tarapith there, it is happening simultaneously," Adhikari said."State-level worship is being held in Tarapith. Here in Kalighat, all our lighting has been set up; it is an atmosphere of celebration throughout," he added.Adhikari said Kolkata holds a special spiritual significance, recalling its association with Maa Kali, Maa Durga, Ramakrishna Paramahansa, Maa Sarada Devi, Swami Vivekananda and Lord Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu."This is a spiritual land. It is the land of Ma Kali, the land of Ma Durga, the land of Thakur Ramakrishna Dev, the land of Ma Sarada Devi, the land of Swami Vivekananda, and the land of Lord Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu," he said.BJP Bengal also posted Adhikari's photo and said, "On the sacred occasion of Kaushiki Amavasya, chief minister Shri Suvendu Adhikari offered prayers to Maa Kali at Kalighat and, following the temple’s traditional customs, partook of the sacred bhog of pulao and fish."This comes days after Bageshwar Dham chief Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, during his visit to West Bengal for a three-day Hanumant Katha in Howrah's Liluah, appealed to Bengali Hindus to observe Navratri with devotion and sincerity.What is the controversyDuring his visit to Bengal, Shastri had appealed to Bengalis to give up non-vegetarian food during the Durga Puja festivities and described those who eat meat on religious occasions as “hypocrites”.Fish and meat are closely associated with traditional cuisine in West Bengal, while religious practices vary across communities and regions.Shastri's remarks also led to a rare display of unity between Congress and BJP as both parties rejected the godman's advice, saying personal views should not dictate what Bengali society should eat.On Tuesday, Congress lodged a police complaint against Shastri, asserting that the call was “intended to create disharmony”.In the complaint submitted to the officer-in-charge of Kolkata’s Bhawanipore police station, the South Kolkata District Congress Committee alleged that Shastri made “derogatory” comments during an event in Howrah on September 5.“We want to apprise you that immediate administrative action needs to be initiated, and an FIR needs to be registered with necessary arrests. His remarks could spark disharmony in society and were against the democratic spirit,” Congress leader Pradip Prasad said in the complaint, according to PTI.Meanwhile, BJP West Bengal chief Samik Bhattacharya said that Bengalis would “continue to eat what they have been eating”.“We generally eat ‘luchi’ on Ashtami and goat meat on Navami. We will continue to do that. Nobody can tell the people of West Bengal what they should eat,” Bhattacharya said.“Let me live the way I want to. Bengalis will eat what they have been eating. Can Bengalis not eat fish and meat?” he asked, quoting Swami Vivekananda.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2017, Hangzhou authorities collected 23,000 abandoned shared bicycles into 16 giant corrals; a green transport boom had created fields of usable bikes
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore the rapid expansion of shared bicycles in Hangzhou, leading to 23,000 abandoned bikes and urban management challenges. Discover the impact of dockless bike-sharing systems on city infrastructure and transportation dynamics.
articles.body: Shared bicycles had spread rapidly across the Chinese city of Hangzhou, with dockless operators letting users leave bikes without returning them to fixed stations. City authorities began removing them when riders abandoned bikes on sidewalks, near transport hubs and in other public spaces.By June 2017, authorities had collected about 23,000 shared bicycles and placed them in 16 makeshift corrals around Hangzhou. Photographs of the storage sites showed thousands of bikes packed together in open lots. The bicycles were still usable in principle, but the problem was that there were suddenly far more of them than the city's streets and parking spaces could accommodate.Hangzhou had already built one of China's largest bike networksHangzhou launched its government-backed public bicycle program in 2008 with the goal of encouraging short-distance cycling and reducing vehicle pollution. The system used designated docking stations, which gave users a clear place to return the bicycles. The arrival of private dockless companies changed that model, as companies such as Ofo and Mobike placed large numbers of bicycles directly on streets. Users could locate a bike with a phone, ride it and leave it near their destination, and that convenience removed the need to return the vehicle to a particular station.A later academic review of China's shared-bicycle networks recorded more than 858,000 bicycles in Hangzhou's government-operated system alone, alongside the much larger fleets of private operators. The city's public bicycle network had more than 3,000 docking stations, and by 2017, the dockless model was creating a second layer of bicycle infrastructure across the city, but without the same physical controls.Parking became a city-management problemA July 2017 report by Shanghai Daily said the city's urban management authority had summoned nine bike-sharing operators and warned them that bicycles needed to be parked inside marked areas. The report said that about 418,000 shared bicycles were operating in Hangzhou at the time and that more than 23,000 had been removed because of random parking. Operators could face fines of up to 20,000 yuan for blocking sidewalks and obstructing traffic.The authorities began marking designated parking areas around places such as hospitals, schools, government buildings, stadiums, museums, libraries, shopping centers and tourist sites. That response tells us about the difficulty of managing dockless bicycles at the scale reached by Hangzhou. The bikes could be placed almost anywhere, but that did not mean every location could absorb them.The corrals became a symbol of oversupplyAccording to WIRED, police and city authorities hauled the bikes to 16 corrals around Hangzhou. Seen from ground level, the sites looked like conventional junkyards, but from above, they became dense fields of brightly colored bicycles. The photographs attracted attention because they turned an invisible logistical problem into a physical landscape.Hangzhou's original public-bike program had been designed around stations and a controlled fleet, but dockless systems removed much of that physical infrastructure in favor of convenience. That meant operators could deploy bicycles quickly, but city authorities had to find new ways to control where the vehicles ended up.The numbers kept changingThe scale of the bicycle boom was difficult to contain because private companies were still adding bikes while authorities were removing them. A 2017 study of Hangzhou's shared-bicycle sector found that the number of shared bicycles in the city's six main districts had already risen above 220,000 by April, and by November, the number had reached 882,700, with daily orders between 800,000 and 1 million.The city had created a transport system capable of putting hundreds of thousands of bicycles into circulation, but then had to build another system for dealing with the vehicles that users left in the wrong places. The abandoned bicycles were not necessarily broken, as many had simply become surplus to the city's available street space. For Hangzhou, the 2017 corrals showed the physical cost of a bike-sharing model that could expand faster than the urban system around it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Corsica's war on the rich: Separatists bomb dozens multimillion-euro properties, warn buyers
articles.summary: News News: On the French island of Corsica, owning a second home can come with an unusual risk of it being blown up by separatists.Corsica’s decades-old independ.
articles.body: On the French island of Corsica, owning a second home can come with an unusual risk of it being blown up by separatists.Corsica’s decades-old independence movement has increasingly turned its attention to second homes, particularly properties owned by people from mainland France and foreign buyers. Since October 2023, dozens of homes have been bombed or set on fire across the island, including 34 properties in 20 towns during a single overnight spree.The campaign has not stopped buyers from coming. Multimillion-euro homes continue to be built and sold, even as separatists warn outsiders against buying property on what they regard as their land.The National Liberation Front of Corsica, or FLNC, the armed wing of the island’s long-running independence movement, has claimed thousands of attacks since it was formed in 1976. The group has increasingly focused on property as part of its campaign against what it sees as the displacement of local Corsicans.Last month, about 15 masked and armed members of the group appeared at a press conference and issued a blunt warning to tourists and prospective second-home buyers.“Until our national rights are recognised and respected, we have only one message to send them,” a member said. “Stay home.”The threat comes against the backdrop of a sharp rise in second-home ownership on the island. A 2026 report by the Corsican Assembly found that second homes account for about 37% of Corsica’s housing stock, rising to as much as 50% in some coastal towns.Despite the attacks, demand for Corsican property remains strong. Real estate agents continue to receive inquiries from prospective buyers, some concerned about the threats and others apparently undeterred.The property attacks are not new. The FLNC claimed responsibility for an operation in 1991 that targeted more than 80 vacation homes. In 2012, masked gunmen reportedly forced a Parisian financier and six others from a villa before blowing it up.The latest wave has prompted a counterterrorism investigation in France. Ten people have been arrested in connection with the 2023 attacks, while prosecutors have also opened a separate investigation into the separatists’ recent press conference.The campaign has coincided with renewed efforts by Paris to address Corsica’s long-standing demands for greater autonomy.The French Senate is due to vote next month on a constitutional amendment recognising Corsica’s distinct language, culture and history while granting its local government additional powers over areas including zoning and waste management.Political scientist André Fazi of the University of Corsica described the separatists’ campaign as a “tactical success”.But the proposed constitutional changes stop short of giving Corsican authorities control over who can buy property on the island, one of the central demands of hardline separatists.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2024, Australian farmers ripped out millions of grapevines while two billion litres of wine sat unsold; some of it was already spoiling in storage
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2024, Australian farmers face an unprecedented wine surplus, leading to the uprooting of millions of grapevines as two billion litres of unsold wine go to waste. This situation is exacerbated by the loss of the lucrative Chinese market and declining red wine demand.
articles.body: Fourth-generation grower James Cremasco watched as vines planted by his grandfather were removed. Millions of vines were being destroyed across Australia, while growers said tens of millions more would have to go as the country struggled with a surplus of wine and falling grape prices.More than two billion litres of unsold wine were sitting in storage, which is equivalent to roughly two years of production, Reuters reported. Some of the stock was already spoiling as producers tried to sell it at heavily reduced prices.The problem had built up over several years, with weaker global wine consumption being compounded by the loss of Australia's lucrative Chinese market.The surplus had become too large for growers to ignoreAustralia is one of the world's major wine-producing and exporting countries, with vineyards spread across dozens of growing regions. The immediate problem in 2024 was particularly severe for red wine, as demand for cheaper red wines had fallen, while Australia's growers were still carrying large areas of vines that were capable of producing more grapes.Reuters reported that some Australian red grapes were selling for little more than A$100 a tonne, while prices had previously reached as much as A$600. In another comparison, the average price for inland red grapes had fallen to A$304 per tonne in 2023, compared with A$659 in 2020. Growers could harvest the crop and still lose money, and some therefore left grapes on the vines, while thers began removing the vines themselves.Griffith became one of the places where the problem was visibleCremasco's decision to remove vines showed the longer-term calculation confronting growers, since keeping an unprofitable vineyard in production still requires irrigation, labor, pruning, harvesting and other costs. If wineries do not want additional grapes, the grower can be left with a crop that has little or no commercial value.Reuters reported that Australia's wine industry estimated as many as 20,000 hectares (about 8% of the country's vineyard area) might need to be removed to restore balance between supply and demand. For individual growers, however, the decision was not simply about industry statistics, as removing established vines meant giving up land that had produced grapes for decades and finding another crop or use for it.China's disappearance from the market made the surplus worseChina had been Australia's most valuable export market for wine before Beijing imposed steep tariffs in 2020, and the trade restrictions sharply reduced exports just as broader global wine consumption was weakening. The Australian wine industry therefore lost an important outlet while vineyards continued producing. Chinese authorities were expected to remove the tariffs by early 2024, but growers and industry representatives did not expect the reopening of the market to immediately absorb the accumulated stock.An ABC Rural report from February 2024 cited Rabobank's estimate of a two-billion-litre oversupply, and also reported that Australia's average inland red-wine grape value had fallen to A$304 per tonne in 2023, which was the lowest recorded level at the time.Growers were being asked to reduce productionGrowers in South Australia's Riverland (another major wine region) called for a moratorium on new plantings in March 2024. An ABC Rural report said the country had accumulated more than two billion litres of excess wine by August 2023, according to Rabobank, and farmers argued that production needed to fall before prices could recover. Higher-value vineyards that served premium markets faced different economics, while large producers were also shifting toward premium wines and reassessing their production.The national stockpile eventually began to decline, with Wine Australia's 2023–24 production and inventory report estimating Australia's wine inventory at 1.96 billion litres as of June 30, 2024, down 228 million litres from the previous year.Most growers were owning vineyards that had been planted by earlier generations, and the arithmetic had become more immediate: keeping vines in the ground meant continuing to produce into an already oversupplied market, while removing them meant abandoning an established source of income. In Griffith, that calculation was visible in rows of uprooted vines and bare soil where vineyards had stood for decades.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
