articles.title: Rs 2 crore extortion call, office firing trigger encounter in Sonipat; 2 injured, 3 pistols recovered
articles.summary: SONIPAT: Sonipat Police launched a crackdown on extortion, firing and illegal arms following a Rs 2-crore extortion demand and subsequent firing at a .
articles.body: SONIPAT: Sonipat Police launched a crackdown on extortion, firing and illegal arms following a Rs 2-crore extortion demand and subsequent firing at a businessman’s office in Kharkhoda.Two alleged assailants were apprehended in an armed encounter after sustaining bullet injuries, police said on Friday.Police claimed to have recovered three country-made pistols and a Bajaj CT-100 motorcycle, allegedly used in the crime, from the accused.The injured suspects were identified as Ankit (21), son of Deepak, a resident of Bhatana village under Mohana police station and currently residing in Pragati Nagar, Sonipat, and Harsh (19), son of Pawan, a resident of Lehrara village under Sadar Sonipat police station.Both were shifted to CHC Kharkhoda for medical treatment.The operation was carried out under the directions of Haryana DGP Ajay Singhal, IPS, and under the guidance of Sonipat police commissioner Mamta Singh, IPS, ADGP, with supervision from DCP Crime Narendra Kadian, IPS.According to Kharkhoda SHO Anil Kumar, the incident began around 9.23pm on September 10, when Kharkhoda resident Deepak received a call from an unidentified number.The caller allegedly claimed to be associated with the Nandu gang and demanded Rs 2 crore in extortion money, threatening to kill Deepak if the money was not paid.Around half an hour after the extortion call, police received information that two to three motorcycle-borne youths had opened fire at Deepak’s office on Khanda Road, Kharkhoda.“On receiving the information, a police team from Kharkhoda police station immediately reached the spot. Given the seriousness of the incident, senior police officers and the concerned CIA and SAUG teams were alerted,” SHO Anil Kumar said.Police said three empty cartridge cases were recovered from the spot, while bullet impact marks were found on the main gate and wall of the office. Investigators collected forensic evidence from the scene and incorporated it into the probe.A case was registered at Kharkhoda police station as FIR No. 509, dated September 11, 2026, at 1.52am, under Sections 287, 3(5) and 308(5) of the BNS and Section 25 of the Arms Act.Following the firing incident, an alert was circulated across the district through the police control room. The SAUG Sector-07 team subsequently launched a pursuit after spotting suspected motorcycle-borne youths.According to police, the chase culminated in an armed confrontation near Harsana village on NH-334B, where the suspects allegedly exchanged fire with the police team.Both suspects sustained bullet injuries during the encounter and were subsequently taken into custody, police said. The two injured accused were later shifted to CHC Kharkhoda for treatment.Police and SAUG personnel recovered three country-made pistols from the accused along with the Bajaj CT-100 motorcycle.Investigators are now attempting to establish the source of the weapons and determine whether the firearms were used in any previous criminal incidents.Police are also probing the alleged criminal network behind the extortion demand and the subsequent attack.Sonipat police spokesperson ASI Ravinder Singh said a separate case had been registered in connection with the alleged firing on the police party during the encounter.“FIR No. 285 dated September 11, 2026 has been registered at Sadar Sonipat police station under Sections 132, 121(1), 221, 109(1) and 3(5) of the BNS and Sections 25/54/59 of the Arms Act,” he said.ACP Crime Rajpal Singh, HPS, said police teams were mobilised immediately after the extortion and firing incidents were reported.He said the SAUG Sector-07 team pursued the suspected motorcycle-borne youths after the alert was circulated through the control room. The pursuit eventually led to the encounter near Harsana, where both suspects were apprehended after sustaining injuries.According to Rajpal Singh, the recovery of three country-made pistols and the motorcycle has added important leads to the investigation.Police are now questioning the accused to establish the source of the weapons, their possible links with other criminals and the larger network allegedly operating behind the extortion bid.The alleged connection with the Nandu gang has emerged as one of the key aspects of the investigation. Police are examining whether the extortion call, the firing at the office and the two arrested suspects are part of a larger organised criminal network.Under the leadership of police commissioner Mamta Singh, IPS, ADGP, Sonipat Police has reiterated its resolve to take stringent action against extortionists, illegal arms dealers, shooters and organised criminal networks operating in the district.Police officials said individuals attempting to terrorise the public through extortion threats or armed attacks would face strict legal action.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: Las Vegas developers bought 940 acres of former federal desert for $94 million; the site is set to become a 6,000-home community with first homes expected in 2028
articles.summary: US News: For years, nearly 940 acres on the northern edge of Las Vegas sat as open federal desert, surrounded by some of Southern Nevada’s most striking landsc.
articles.body: For years, nearly 940 acres on the northern edge of Las Vegas sat as open federal desert, surrounded by some of Southern Nevada’s most striking landscapes. Now, the vast stretch of undeveloped land is set to become a new city-within-a-city, with plans for as many as 6,000 homes, schools, parks, commercial areas and dedicated housing for military and workforce families.The $94 million land deal has cleared the way for Monument Hills, a master-planned community in the upper northwest Las Vegas Valley. The project is being developed by Olympia Companies and Bruin Capital Partners, which acquired the roughly 940-acre site after a federal land transaction involving the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and the City of Las Vegas. The first homes are expected to arrive around spring 2028, although the entire development is likely to take years to build out.From federal desert to a massive residential neighbourhoodThe property lies between the Las Vegas Paiute Tribe’s Snow Mountain Reservation to the west and Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument to the east, putting the future community at the edge of the rapidly expanding Las Vegas metropolitan area. It is also near US Highway 95, an important route connecting the area with the rest of the valley.The BLM finalised the sale of the public land in late August, with the City of Las Vegas then conveying it to the developers. The $94 million transaction was conducted at appraised fair-market value under the Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act, which allows certain federal lands within the Las Vegas Valley disposal boundary to be sold for development.The transaction is significant even by Las Vegas standards. According to Nevada officials, it represents the largest BLM land transaction in the Las Vegas Valley in more than two decades.The developers are planning Monument Hills as more than a collection of suburban housing tracts. The approved plans allocate space for residential neighbourhoods, commercial uses, schools, parks, trails and other public facilities. City planning documents allow a maximum of 6,000 dwelling units across the development.6,000 homes across three villagesMonument Hills is expected to contain up to 6,000 homes spread across three villages. The housing is planned to cover multiple segments of the market, from more attainable housing to higher-end executive homes.The project also includes provisions for military and workforce housing. Current plans call for hundreds of units intended to serve those segments, including housing connected to the needs of personnel at nearby military installations.The community will not be residential-only. Development plans include two school sites, commercial and mixed-use areas, public facilities and roughly 90 acres dedicated to parks, trails and open space.That mix is designed to turn what is currently an expanse of desert into a functioning neighbourhood where residents can live, study, shop and spend time outdoors without having to travel across the valley for every service.Why Las Vegas is turning to federal landThe development comes as Southern Nevada continues to grapple with a housing shortage while its population grows. The BLM said the region is projected to add hundreds of thousands of residents over the next decade. Clark County officials have also identified a shortfall of tens of thousands of housing units needed to accommodate current demand and anticipated population growth.Las Vegas has increasingly looked toward federal land as one way to create room for that expansion. Much of the land surrounding the valley is federally managed, meaning large-scale development often depends on federal land-disposal decisions.The Monument Hills transaction is therefore not simply a real estate deal. It represents the conversion of public desert into privately developed housing at a time when local governments are searching for ways to increase the supply of homes.Where will the $94 million go?Although the development will ultimately put the land into private hands, the federal sale is also expected to generate public benefits across Nevada.Under the rules governing the transaction, 85% of the proceeds will support projects throughout the state, including parks, trails and natural areas, improvements on federal lands, environmentally sensitive land acquisitions, wildfire-resilience projects and landscape restoration. Another 5% will go to the state for education, while 10% will be directed to the Southern Nevada Water Authority. That means the sale of the desert acreage is expected to fund projects well beyond the future boundaries of Monument Hills.When will people actually move in?Despite the size of the announcement, the community is still years away from becoming a neighbourhood filled with residents. The first homes are expected around spring 2028. Current development information indicates that ground has not yet been broken and homebuilders have not been announced, meaning buyers cannot purchase homes in Monument Hills yet.The transformation, however, could dramatically alter the northwest edge of Las Vegas. What is now largely open desert will eventually contain thousands of homes, roads, schools, parks and commercial areas. The project is also expected to generate substantial construction activity and long-term economic activity as the community takes shape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A quarter century after 9/11: 25 ways America's darkest day changed the world
articles.summary: US News: Twenty-five years ago America saw the darkest chapter in its history and the world hasn't been the same since.On September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijac.
articles.body: Twenty-five years ago America saw the darkest chapter in its history and the world hasn't been the same since.On September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers seized four commercial aircraft and turned them into weapons. Two planes crashed into New York's World Trade Center, one struck the Pentagon and a fourth crashed into a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. The attacks killed 2,977 people from 90 countries and changed the course of American foreign policy and global politics.The US invaded Afghanistan weeks later and Iraq less than two years after that. But the legacy of 9/11 reached far beyond those wars. Governments expanded surveillance and border controls. Airports became more heavily securitised. Intelligence agencies changed how they shared information. Drones transformed warfare, while the internet transformed terrorist recruitment. Islamophobia and debates over immigration intensified. America's global standing was damaged, while China's rise continued.Here's how 9/11 changed the world in 25 ways:1. Governments learned to watch their own citizensThe post-9/11 security state did more than give governments new powers; it changed expectations about privacy. The USA PATRIOT Act expanded US authorities' ability to access communications, financial records and other information in terrorism investigations. Later revelations about the collection of telephone and internet data showed how far surveillance had expanded. Other countries introduced or strengthened their own intelligence powers. The lasting shift was the growing acceptance that governments could collect and analyse enormous amounts of data in the name of preventing terrorism, even when most of the people being monitored were not suspected of any crime.2. Flying became a security ritualAir travel changed almost overnight. Screening became more extensive, passenger information was checked against watchlists, and procedures such as shoe removal, liquid restrictions, enhanced searches and full-body scanning became familiar to travellers. The creation of the Transportation Security Administration in the US put airport screening under federal control.3. A new security bureaucracy was builtThe US created the Department of Homeland Security in 2003, bringing together 22 federal departments and agencies. Its responsibilities stretched from airport and border security to emergency preparedness and protection of critical infrastructure. The change reflected a broader shift in how governments understood national security. Terrorism was no longer seen only as an overseas military or intelligence problem. Protecting the homeland became a permanent task involving airports, borders, transport systems, public spaces and local authorities.4. Intelligence sharing became a priorityOne of the clearest lessons of 9/11 was that important pieces of information existed before the attacks but were not effectively connected. US agencies subsequently changed how they shared intelligence, including through the creation of the Director of National Intelligence in 2004. Databases, watchlists and information-sharing systems became more integrated, while cooperation between intelligence and law-enforcement agencies expanded. Internationally, governments exchanged more information about suspected militants, travel and financial activity.5. Money became a weapon and a targetTerrorism was increasingly treated as a financial problem as well as a military one. Governments pushed banks to identify customers, report suspicious transactions and trace money linked to extremist networks. The US Treasury gained powerful tools for freezing assets and imposing financial sanctions. These measures helped make terrorist financing harder, but they also transformed ordinary banking. International transfers, charity payments and opening accounts became subject to layers of identity and compliance checks.6. Afghanistan became America's longest warWithin a month of the attacks, the US and its allies invaded Afghanistan to dismantle al-Qaeda and remove the Taliban government that had sheltered Osama bin Laden. The Taliban fell quickly, but the war did not. What began as a campaign against al-Qaeda became a two-decade effort involving counter-insurgency, nation-building and repeated Taliban offensives. The US withdrawal in 2021 was followed by the Taliban's rapid return to power. The episode became one of the defining questions of the post-9/11 era: what does victory look like in a war against a network rather than a conventional army?7. Iraq destabilised the Middle EastThe 2003 invasion of Iraq widened the consequences of 9/11 far beyond Afghanistan. Saddam Hussein was removed, but the failure to find the stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction used to justify the invasion badly damaged trust in the war's rationale. Iraq then endured insurgency, sectarian violence and political instability. The conflict weakened existing regional structures and created space for armed groups to grow. The invasion became a turning point in Middle Eastern politics, demonstrating how quickly the removal of one government could produce consequences that spread far beyond the battlefield.8. Isis showed how one war could produce another threatThe instability that followed the Iraq war helped create the conditions in which Islamic State emerged. By 2014, Isis controlled large areas of Iraq and Syria and proclaimed a caliphate. Its brutality was only one part of its power: it also became adept at online propaganda, recruitment and the use of social media. The group eventually lost its territorial state, but its rise showed how counter-terrorism campaigns could generate new security threats.9. War moved further away from the battlefieldThe post-9/11 wars helped normalise a form of warfare in which a country could target suspected militants without sending large numbers of troops into battle. Armed drones became central to US operations in Pakistan, Yemen and Somalia, allowing strikes against targets thousands of kilometres from American bases. The technology reduced risks to soldiers and made some operations easier to conduct, but it also raised difficult questions about civilian casualties, intelligence failures and legal accountability.10. Iran gained greater regional influenceThe overthrow of Saddam Hussein in 2003 removed one of Iran's most important regional rivals. Iraq's subsequent political instability created space for Iran to expand its influence through political allies and armed groups. The Syrian war later deepened this shift, drawing Iran, Russia, Turkey, Gulf states and the US into a complex regional struggle. The result was a Middle East in which power became more fragmented and non-state armed groups played a larger role.11. Nato and counter-terrorism became global projectsFor the first time, NATO invoked Article 5, treating the 9/11 attacks as an attack on all its members. European allies and other countries joined the campaign in Afghanistan. Intelligence agencies expanded international cooperation, police forces created counter-terrorism units and governments coordinated watchlists and border controls. The result was a more interconnected security architecture. Yet the alliance was not immune to disagreement: controversies over detainees, drone strikes and the Iraq war exposed the limits of a global coalition built around a single threat.12 America's image took a lasting hitThe US emerged from 9/11 with enormous international sympathy. That goodwill weakened as the wars dragged on and controversies over Guantanamo Bay, Abu Ghraib, interrogation practices and Iraq's weapons of mass destruction damaged Washington's credibility. Allies became more critical of American policy, while opponents used the wars to challenge US claims about democracy and human rights. Military power remained immense, but the post-9/11 period showed that even the world's most powerful country could struggle to turn military victories into political legitimacy and international trust.13. China's rise gained strategic spaceChina's rise was already under way before 9/11. But the timing mattered. Beijing joined the World Trade Organisation in December 2001 and then experienced two decades of rapid economic expansion while Washington devoted enormous political, military and financial resources to Afghanistan, Iraq and the wider fight against terrorism. China's growing role in global trade and finance eventually translated into greater strategic influence. By the 2020s, the US increasingly viewed China, rather than jihadist terrorism, as its principal long-term strategic competitor. 9/11 did not cause China's rise, but it formed part of the geopolitical backdrop against which that rise accelerated.14. Borders became harder to crossCounter-terrorism changed immigration and border control. Biometric identification, passenger databases, watchlists, more intensive visa checks and no-fly lists became standard features of travel in many countries. Measures originally designed to identify terrorism suspects increasingly became part of wider migration and border systems. For legitimate travellers, the change was often experienced as paperwork, interviews, fingerprints and longer checks. The deeper change was political: security became a central part of the debate over who should be allowed to enter, settle and move across borders.15. Islamophobia became a lasting consequenceThe attacks were carried out by 19 extremists, but suspicion and hostility often spread far beyond the perpetrators. In the US, reported anti-Muslim hate crimes rose sharply in 2001. Muslim and South Asian communities faced increased scrutiny, discrimination and hostility, including during travel and at workplaces. Across Western countries, terrorism became increasingly linked in political debate with immigration and Islam. The consequence was a lasting social divide: an attack carried out by a small extremist organisation contributed to a broader suspicion of millions of people who had no connection to it.16. Civil liberties came under pressureThe central political argument after 9/11 was simple but difficult: how much freedom should societies surrender in exchange for greater security? Expanded surveillance, detention without trial, interrogation programmes and broader police powers all became part of the debate. Supporters argued that exceptional threats required exceptional tools. Critics warned that temporary emergency measures could become permanent. Twenty-five years later, the argument remains unresolved.17. Guantanamo became a symbol of the eraThe detention facility at Guantanamo Bay became one of the most recognisable symbols of the post-9/11 security system. Hundreds of suspected enemy combatants were held there, often for years without conventional criminal trials. The prison generated international criticism over due process, interrogation and indefinite detention. Attempts to close it repeatedly stalled. Its importance goes beyond the number of prisoners who remain there. Guantanamo became shorthand for a broader question: can a democracy fight terrorism while maintaining the legal principles it claims to defend?18. The wars created a huge displacement crisisThe human consequences of the post-9/11 wars extended far beyond the countries where Western troops fought. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that more than 38 million people were displaced by wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, the Philippines, Libya and Syria. Millions crossed international borders, while many more were displaced within their own countries. The resulting refugee and migration pressures affected neighbouring states and reshaped political debates in Europe and elsewhere.19. First responders paid a price that lasted decadesThe human cost of 9/11 did not end when the fires at Ground Zero were extinguished. Dust and toxic substances exposed responders, survivors and residents to long-term health risks. Thousands have since developed illnesses recognised as linked to the attacks and their aftermath. The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act, passed in 2010 and later made permanent, created long-term support for affected responders and survivors.20. Ground Zero became a global site of remembranceThe physical site of the attacks was transformed into a place of mourning. The 9/11 Memorial opened in 2011, followed by the museum in 2014. Two reflecting pools occupy the footprints of the Twin Towers, with the names of the victims inscribed around them. Every year, families gather to read those names. After 25 years of arguments over war, surveillance and security, the memorial serves a different purpose: it brings the story back to the people who died. The remembrance is deliberately personal rather than political.21. Terrorism moved online The internet transformed the terrorist threat after 9/11. In 2001, extremist propaganda still depended heavily on traditional media. By the time ISIS emerged, militant groups could produce sophisticated videos, distribute propaganda instantly and reach potential recruits directly through social platforms and encrypted services. Governments consequently had to fight terrorism in a new environment where borders mattered less and information travelled globally in seconds. The battle was no longer only about finding people in physical networks; it was also about tracking ideas, recruitment and propaganda online.22: Snowden and WikiLeaksThe post-9/11 security apparatus eventually produced a new question: who was watching the watchers? WikiLeaks' publication of classified US military and diplomatic documents, followed by Edward Snowden's disclosures in 2013 about mass electronic surveillance, exposed the extraordinary scale of government secrecy and data collection. The revelations showed how counter-terrorism programmes had expanded far beyond traditional spying on suspected militants. They triggered fierce debates over privacy, government transparency and the responsibilities of whistleblowers. Governments argued that such disclosures endangered national security; supporters said the public had a right to know what was being done in its name.23. Pop culture resetThe post-9/11 world changed not only government policy but also the stories people consumed. Films, television shows and video games increasingly revolved around terrorism, surveillance, soldiers, intelligence agencies and threats from within. Characters were often forced to make impossible choices between individual rights and public safety — mirroring arguments taking place in the real world. The culture of permanent threat became familiar entertainment. Over time, the fictional world of terrorist plots, security alerts and surveillance began to resemble the assumptions of everyday life.24. Information became a new battlefieldThe post-9/11 era also changed how governments and political movements fought for influence. Terrorist groups used the internet for propaganda and recruitment, while states increasingly recognised that controlling information could be as important as controlling territory. Social media later allowed governments, political groups and foreign actors to reach millions of people directly, often without traditional media acting as a filter. Disinformation, manipulated narratives and online influence campaigns became tools of political competition. The result was a world in which a conflict could be fought not only with soldiers, missiles or sanctions, but with videos, social-media posts and competing versions of reality.25. The costs will continue long after the warsThe financial consequences of 9/11 did not end when troops left Afghanistan or the main fighting in Iraq subsided. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that the US spent or committed about $8 trillion on post-9/11 wars through 2021–22, including future obligations for veterans. It estimates that healthcare and other costs for post-9/11 veterans could reach $2.2 trillion to $2.5 trillion by 2050. The final cost therefore cannot be measured only in military spending. It includes veterans' care, interest payments, lost lives, displacement and other consequences that will continue for decades. The wars may have ended, but their bills have not.Where we are, 25 years laterTwenty-five years after 9/11, its legacy cannot be reduced to the destruction of the Twin Towers or the wars that followed. The attacks changed institutions, laws, borders, technology and the way governments understood security. They altered America's place in the world and reshaped politics far beyond its borders.The consequences were also measured in lives far from New York and Washington: soldiers killed, civilians displaced, communities divided and first responders who continued to suffer years after the smoke cleared.The most lasting legacy may be this: an event that lasted hours created assumptions about security, war and power that have lasted a quarter century.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Houthis' coastal offensive puts Bab el-Mandeb in crosshairs; why the strait matters
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran-backed Houthis have taken control of a Yemeni island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, according to officials cited by .
articles.body: Iran-backed Houthis have taken control of a Yemeni island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, according to officials cited by the Associated Press, giving the group a direct foothold in the strategic waterway and raising fresh concerns over the safety of global shipping.The Houthis have also captured Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Mocha and are advancing south towards the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, marking a major escalation in the country’s long-running war.The group has moved against the Hanish Islands, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have withdrawn towards Dhubab, a coastal town located directly on the strait, opposite Perim Island.According to Yemeni government sources cited by Reuters, “Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait.”Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the strait remained safe, but added that Houthi operations would continue until the “aggression” against Yemen ends.The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center said navigation remained safe for all shipping companies except Saudi vessels, which remain subject to a previously announced ban.UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg told the UN Security Council on Thursday that the international community must act to address the escalating conflict. Grundberg said the Houthis’ control of Mocha gives them "a direct presence on the approaches to one of the world’s most vital straits", raising serious concerns over freedom of navigation and maritime trade security.The US representative at the meeting, Jenifer Neidhart de Ortiz, accused the Houthis of acting as "agents and tools of Iran", saying: “This escalation is unacceptable, and those who enable it bear responsibility for its consequences.”Iran’s foreign ministry, meanwhile, said the Yemen conflict could not be resolved through a blockade or military action against the Houthis and called for dialogue, without addressing Tehran’s own role in supporting the group.Why Bab el-Mandeb mattersThe Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, connecting the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden to one of the world’s main Asia-Europe shipping routes. Its importance has grown further as vessels have increasingly relied on the Red Sea as an alternative route amid disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates that 8.1 million barrels per day of crude oil, condensate and petroleum products passed through Bab el-Mandeb in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.4 million bpd in the previous quarter. That was roughly 8 percent of global oil supply during the period.For global trade, any sustained Houthi control of, or disruption to, the strait could force shipping companies to avoid the Red Sea and Suez Canal and reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope.That longer journey means higher fuel consumption, freight and insurance costs, as well as longer delivery times. Major carriers took this step previously after a series of Houthi attacks made Red Sea shipping too risky.Saudi Arabia faces a dual maritime threat. The Houthis have warned that they will target Saudi vessels in the Red Sea, while disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz threaten another key route for Saudi oil exports.How Yemen descended into a decade-long warYemen’s war began after years of political instability and a failed political transition following the 2011 uprising. The Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee.Saudi Arabia intervened in 2015 to support Hadi’s government, turning the conflict into a regional war involving the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-led forces.The war has killed tens of thousands of people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. In 2026, the UN estimates that 22.3 million people need humanitarian assistance, including 18.3 million facing acute food insecurity. More than 6 million people are at emergency levels of food deprivation.A UN-brokered truce in 2022 reduced fighting but failed to deliver a lasting peace. The Houthis later expanded the conflict beyond Yemen by attacking commercial ships in the Red Sea following the outbreak of the Israel-Gaza war in 2023, making Yemen a key flashpoint in the wider Middle East conflict.The latest coastal offensive now adds a new dimension to the crisis. By pushing towards Bab el-Mandeb, the Houthis are moving closer to a chokepoint whose disruption could have consequences far beyond Yemen, threatening shipping, energy flows and supply chains linking Asia, the Middle East and Europe.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian national charged in US for allegedly posing as American to vote
articles.summary: US News: An Indian national has been indicted in the US for allegedly falsely claiming to be an American citizen in order to vote in the 2024 general election..
articles.body: An Indian national has been indicted in the US for allegedly falsely claiming to be an American citizen in order to vote in the 2024 general election.Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari was charged by a federal grand jury in Minnesota with two counts related to allegedly making a false claim of US citizenship to vote, according to the US Department of Justice.What does the indictment allege?According to the DOJ, Chaudhari signed a voter signature certificate in Minnesota on November 5, 2024, when he voted in the US general election. The certificate required voters to swear or affirm that they were US citizens.The indictment alleges that Chaudhari was not a US citizen but knowingly made the false citizenship statement in order to cast his ballot.What are the charges against Chaudhari?Chaudhari faces two federal charges. One count alleges that he provided false information in voting, while the other accuses him of making a false claim of US citizenship in order to register to vote or vote.If convicted, he could face a maximum sentence of five years in prison on each count. Any sentence would be decided by a federal district judge after considering the US Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.Who is Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari?The DOJ identifies Chaudhari as an Indian national. Its September 10 announcement did not provide further details about his age, occupation, immigration status or how long he has been in the US.The case is being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, with assistance from the Fillmore County Sheriff's Office.Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division said the department would hold accountable people who knowingly make false claims of citizenship to vote.An indictment is an allegation, and Chaudhari is presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. The commander of Hamas's Khan Yunis Brigade, Muhammad Yazouri, was killed in an Israeli Air Force strike in Khan Yunis, along with two other Hamas terrorists.

The strike targeted a vehicle in the Hamad neighborhood, north of Khan Yunis, causing a residential apartment in Tower M to catch fire.

Israeli security forces also eliminated Hamas terrorist Farah Hamed, responsible for deadly attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers, in a joint operation in the central Gaza Strip.

A Thursday overnight Israeli Air Force strike in Khan Yunis killed the commander of Hamas's Khan Yunis Brigade, Muhammad Yazouri, the IDF announced on Friday.

The IDF stated that, before becoming the commander of the brigade, Yazouri had been Deputy Commander of the Khan Younis Brigade, Commander of the Combat Support Battalion, and Head of the Brigade's Intelligence Department.

According to the IDF, the same strike had also killed Hudheifa Muammar, a company commander, and Muhammad Bahjat Rashi, another Hamas terrorist.

IDF, Shin Bet, Israel Police kills Hamas terrorist responsible for 2002 shooting

Hamed was killed on Wednesday in a joint Shin Bet , IDF, and Israel Police operation involving a strike in the central Gaza Strip, according to the security agencies.

articles.title: Brics summit: PM Modi gifts Putin Russian translation of Thirukkural
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday gifted Russian President Vladimir Putin a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the ancient Tamil .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday gifted Russian President Vladimir Putin a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the ancient Tamil classic by poet-philosopher Thiruvalluvar, during their bilateral meeting in New Delhi ahead of the Brics Summit.The edition, published in 2026 by the Central Institute of Classical Tamil, has been translated into Russian by Naira Mkrtchyan. The institute lists the volume as part of its Thirukkural translation series."Presented President Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, which carries the eternal wisdom of the great Thiruvalluvar across languages and borders," PM Modi said on X.The Thirukkural is one of the best-known works of classical Tamil literature. The work covers themes ranging from ethics and governance to friendship, justice and personal conduct, and has been translated into several languages.PM Modi and Putin held bilateral talks at Bharat Mandapam on Friday, a day before the two-day Brics Summit begins in New Delhi. Putin arrived in the capital earlier in the day on a three-day visit to India.The talks come amid efforts by India and Russia to deepen cooperation across defence, energy, trade and civil nuclear power.Defence is expected to remain a key part of the engagement. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said the two sides are exploring upgrades to the BrahMos missile system, while Russia remains committed to completing deliveries of the S-400 air-defence system and has also been discussing the possible supply of Su-57 fighter jets to India.Energy and nuclear cooperation are also on the agenda, with Moscow looking to expand its role in India's civil nuclear programme.PM Modi and Putin had last met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, where the Ukraine conflict was among the issues discussed.The Brics Summit will be held in New Delhi on September 12-13, with leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian among those attending.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian man on student visa in US sentenced to 30 months for defrauding Vietnam veteran
articles.summary: US News: An Indian citizen living in the US on a student visa has been sentenced to 30 months in prison for his role in a scheme that defrauded an elderly Viet.
articles.body: An Indian citizen living in the US on a student visa has been sentenced to 30 months in prison for his role in a scheme that defrauded an elderly Vietnam veteran, the US Attorney’s Office said.Venkateswara Chagamreddy, 37, of San Antonio, Texas, was also ordered to pay USD 99,496 in restitution and will serve three years of supervised release after his prison term. He is expected to face removal proceedings from the US after completing his sentence.A federal jury convicted Chagamreddy in April 2026 of conspiring to defraud the elderly veteran. He will remain in custody pending his transfer to the US Bureau of Prisons.How did the fraud scheme work?The case began in August 2025 when the elderly victim called a phone number he believed was Microsoft support. The person answering falsely told him that criminal activity had been detected on his computer and that the matter would be reported to the federal government.The victim was then contacted by a person posing as a federal officer, who claimed that his identity had been stolen and used to commit federal crimes. He was later transferred to someone posing as a Treasury Department official.The fake official told the victim to convert his money into gold and said an officer would come to collect it. The victim followed the instructions, sent photographs of the gold and handed over the package to the person who arrived to collect it.Days later, the fake officer demanded more money. The victim then contacted a family member, who realised he was being scammed and alerted the Delaware County Sheriff’s Office.How was Chagamreddy caught?With the victim’s cooperation, deputies arranged another gold pickup. Chagamreddy arrived at the victim’s home at the scheduled time and was arrested.Authorities found $500 in cash, a cellphone and 23 ounces of gold in his vehicle, the US Attorney’s Office said.Evidence presented at trial showed that Chagamreddy had been communicating with another person involved in the fraud scheme and had travelled across several states to collect gold from elderly victims.According to evidence presented to the jury, Chagamreddy flew from Austin to North Carolina, where he picked up gold from an 87-year-old woman. He later travelled to Kansas, where he collected another 23 ounces of gold from a 75-year-old woman.He then drove to Delaware County, Oklahoma, where the 79-year-old Vietnam veteran lived alone on a rural road. Messages recovered from Chagamreddy’s phone showed that the alleged co-conspirator had sent him a photograph of the victim, who was wearing a Vietnam veteran shirt.The US Attorney’s Office said the evidence showed Chagamreddy worked with another person to target multiple victims within a 48-hour period.US Attorney Christopher J Nassar said elder-fraud schemes use fear and deception to target vulnerable people. He said Chagamreddy, an Indian national in the US on a student visa, used fear to deceive and extort a Vietnam veteran.The case was investigated by the Delaware County Sheriff’s Office, Homeland Security Investigations and the Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office.
